posts.title: The retention audit starts before the campaign

copy.default:
Most retention work starts too late.

The business sees a quiet diary and asks:

“What campaign should we send?”

I would start earlier.

Who finished an appointment without another one booked?
Who is now outside their normal return window?
Which cancellations never recovered?
Which enquiries showed intent but never became appointments?
Where is useful capacity repeatedly sitting empty?

Those are five different states.

They should not all get the same message.

The first job of a retention audit is not writing copy.

It is finding where the client journey stopped behaving the way the business expected.

Once you know the state, the next action becomes much easier to judge.

Sometimes it is follow-up.

Sometimes it is a booking change.

Sometimes it is a staff handoff.

Sometimes the correct answer is to do nothing.

Diagnosis first.

Automation second.

posts.title: The system I want 222Emails to become

copy.default:
I do not want 222Emails to become “the company that sends more emails”.

That would be too small.

The system I am trying to build is closer to this:

A business can see where clients are dropping out.

It knows which gaps are worth acting on.

It knows who should hear from them, why, and when.

It knows what should stop the journey.

And it can tell whether the action actually brought somebody back.

Email might be part of that.

So might SMS.

So might a booking change, a waitlist, a staff task or no automation at all.

That is why I keep using the phrase Client Return System.

The goal is not more messages.

The goal is fewer valuable client relationships quietly disappearing between appointments.

posts.title: The client did not become a bad lead

copy.default:
A client can enquire, sound interested, and still never book.

That does not automatically make them a bad lead.

Something happened between intent and appointment.

Maybe the reply came too late.

Maybe the next step was unclear.

Maybe the right time was unavailable.

Maybe they needed reassurance.

Maybe they simply got distracted.

Maybe the business never followed up.

The useful question is not:

“Why are our leads poor?”

It is:

“Where did the journey stop?”

That question is less convenient because it forces the business to inspect its own process.

But it is also more useful.

If the leak is happening after intent already exists, buying more leads can make the problem more expensive without fixing it.

posts.title: A full diary can still hide a retention leak

copy.default:
A full diary is good news.

It is not proof that retention is healthy.

You can be busy while still losing clients who should have returned.

New enquiries can keep replacing them.

Promotions can keep filling gaps.

A small group of loyal clients can carry a large share of the bookings.

Meanwhile:

First-time clients leave without rebooking.
Regulars stretch further between visits.
Cancellations disappear.
Dormant clients keep growing.
Quiet hours repeat every week.

The diary shows occupancy.

It does not automatically show the health of the client base underneath it.

That is why I would never judge retention from “we are fully booked” alone.

I would want to know who is returning, how often, where the journey breaks, and how much of today’s demand depends on constantly replacing yesterday’s clients.

posts.title: The hardest part of automation is deciding who should not get it

copy.default:
The easiest part of automation is sending.

The harder part is exclusion.

Who should not enter the workflow?

Who has already booked?

Who is in a live conversation with a member of staff?

Who explicitly said no?

Who opted out?

Who is no longer relevant to the journey?

Who has moved into a different client state?

Without those rules, automation can be technically perfect and commercially clumsy.

That is why I increasingly think good lifecycle design starts with boundaries.

Trigger.

Eligibility.

Exclusions.

Stop conditions.

Human handoff.

Then the message.

The point is not to automate every possible touchpoint.

It is to make the useful ones happen consistently without losing context.

posts.title: What would make you rebook before leaving?

copy.default:
A question for anyone who runs or works inside an appointment business:

What actually makes clients rebook before they leave?

Not what the software says should happen.

What works in practice?

Is it the practitioner asking at the right moment?

A clear recommendation for when to return?

Making the next appointment part of the checkout?

A small incentive?

Limited availability?

A reminder after the visit?

Something else?

I am interested because “no rebook” is easy to treat as a messaging problem.

But the strongest answer might be operational.

The best follow-up can sometimes be making the next step obvious while the client is still there.

Curious what you see working in the real world.

posts.title: An inactive client is not a useful enough label

copy.default:
“Inactive client” sounds precise.

It often is not.

A client who normally returns every four weeks and is now at week seven is different from somebody who visited once eighteen months ago.

Both can sit inside the same inactive segment.

Only one may have just moved outside their normal pattern.

That matters because timing changes the meaning of follow-up.

The better question is:

What was normal for this client or service?

When did they move outside that range?

Is contact useful now?

The more accurately a business defines client states, the less it has to rely on blanket win-back campaigns.

Good retention work is often less about sending more.

It is about knowing exactly who has changed state and why that matters.

posts.title: I am building Retention School around one constraint

copy.default:
I am building Retention School around one constraint:

An appointment-led business owner should not need a marketing dictionary to understand where revenue is leaking.

So instead of starting with lifecycle terminology, I want to start with moments they already recognise.

A client leaves without rebooking.

A regular quietly stops returning.

An enquiry never becomes an appointment.

A cancellation creates an empty slot.

Useful capacity sits unused.

Those are understandable without any jargon.

The system underneath can still be sophisticated.

Segmentation.

Triggers.

Stop logic.

Attribution.

CRM structure.

Automation.

But the problem should stay simple enough to see.

If I cannot explain the leak clearly before explaining the solution, I probably have not simplified it enough yet.

posts.title: The best retention message might be no message

copy.default:
Sometimes the best retention message is no message.

That sounds strange coming from someone who works with lifecycle systems.

But not every dormant client needs chasing.

Not every quiet period is a retention problem.

Not every enquiry is still commercially relevant.

Not every cancellation should trigger a sequence.

Sometimes the data is weak.

Sometimes the timing has passed.

Sometimes the customer has already made their preference clear.

Sometimes the real problem is elsewhere.

A good system should be allowed to decide:

“No action needed.”

That is one of the differences between automation and judgement.

Automation asks:

“Can we send this?”

Judgement asks:

“Should we?”

posts.title: A cancellation is a revenue event, not just an admin event

copy.default:
A cancellation usually gets treated as an admin event.

Remove appointment.

Free the slot.

Maybe send a confirmation.

Done.

Commercially, more happened than that.

A client who had enough intent to book is now unbooked.

Capacity has reopened.

There may be another client who wanted that time.

The original client may still want the service at a different time.

Those are separate recovery paths.

So I would want to know:

Can the slot be refilled?

Does the client need a rebooking route?

Should a waitlist be activated?

When does the opportunity expire?

A cancellation policy helps manage behaviour.

A cancellation recovery system helps manage what happens next.

posts.title: The CRM field test I keep coming back to

copy.default:
I keep coming back to one test for CRM fields:

What decision becomes better because this exists?

If the answer is none, the field may just be administrative decoration.

For a Client Return System, useful data should help answer things like:

What state is this client in?

What happened last time?

When should the business act?

Who owns the next step?

What should stop the workflow?

Did the client actually return?

More fields do not automatically create more intelligence.

The goal is not to collect everything.

It is to capture enough truth to make the next decision better.

That is a much higher bar than “we have the data somewhere”.

posts.title: What booking software should show you next

copy.default:
If I could add one screen to every appointment-booking platform, it would not be another bookings dashboard.

It would be a Client Return dashboard.

I would want to see:

Clients who left without rebooking.

Clients now overdue versus their normal return pattern.

Cancellations still unresolved.

No-shows with no next appointment.

Enquiries that never converted.

Repeated empty-capacity windows.

And one more thing:

What happened after the business acted?

Because “we sent the reminder” is not the outcome.

The outcome is whether the client returned, booked, replied, declined, or moved into a different state.

Booking software already knows a lot about what happened.

The opportunity is making the next commercially useful action easier to see.

posts.title: No-show prevention and no-show recovery are different systems

copy.default:
No-show prevention and no-show recovery are not the same job.

Prevention happens before the appointment.

Clear confirmations.

Useful reminders.

Easy rescheduling.

Deposit or policy logic where appropriate.

Recovery starts after the appointment was missed.

Is the client still suitable to rebook?

Should staff intervene?

Is there a fee or policy step?

What should happen if they rebook?

When should follow-up stop?

The mistake is treating both as one “reminder problem”.

They happen at different moments and need different logic.

A reminder can reduce the chance of a no-show.

It cannot decide what the business should do once the no-show has already happened.

That needs its own recovery path.

posts.title: Final year starts soon, and this is what I want to get better at

copy.default:
My final year of university starts soon.

One thing I want to get much better at this year is turning theory into operating systems.

Not just understanding a framework.

Using it.

Testing it.

Finding where it breaks.

Measuring what changed.

That is probably why I have become so interested in retention and revenue recovery.

The interesting part is not knowing that repeat customers matter.

Everybody already knows that.

The interesting part is building the process that notices when a valuable relationship starts drifting, decides whether action is useful, and measures what happened next.

That is the skill I want to keep sharpening this year:

Less “I understand the concept”.

More “I can make the concept work in the real world”.

posts.title: The quietest revenue leak is often the client who meant to come back

copy.default:
One of the quietest revenue leaks is the client who fully intended to come back.

They liked the service.

Nothing went wrong.

They just did not book the next appointment.

Then work got busy.

A few weeks passed.

The normal return point went by.

The business assumed they would return when ready.

The client assumed they would remember.

Neither side did anything wrong.

The relationship simply drifted.

That is why retention is not only a satisfaction problem.

It is also a timing, memory and friction problem.

A good return system is not there to pressure somebody into buying.

It is there to make the sensible next step easier before a good relationship quietly becomes a dormant one.

posts.title: Empty capacity deserves a diagnosis before a discount

copy.default:
An empty appointment slot does not automatically mean the price is wrong.

Before discounting it, I would want to know why the capacity is empty.

Was demand never there?

Did somebody cancel?

Was there a waitlist that never got activated?

Are regular clients overdue?

Are enquiries getting stuck before booking?

Is that time simply unpopular every week?

Those causes point to different actions.

Discounting is one lever.

It should not be the diagnosis.

If the real issue is a broken return or recovery path, cheaper appointments can hide the leak rather than fix it.

The right question is not:

“How do we fill this slot?”

It is:

“Why is this slot empty, and what type of problem are we actually solving?”

posts.title: The metric I care about more than sends

copy.default:
I care much less about how many follow-up messages a system sends than I used to.

A send is an activity.

It is not an outcome.

The questions I care about more are:

Did the client book?

Did they reply?

Did they decline?

Did a staff member take over?

Did the slot get recovered?

Did the client move back into an active return pattern?

Did the system stop when it should?

Those answers tell you whether the journey changed.

Open rates and clicks can still be useful diagnostics.

But a Client Return System should eventually be judged by what happened to the client relationship and the commercial outcome.

Otherwise the business can optimise the messaging while the actual leak stays exactly where it was.

posts.title: Five leaks. Which one would you check first?

copy.default:
If you had 30 minutes inside an appointment business, which leak would you check first?

1. Clients leaving without rebooking.

2. Regulars who are now overdue.

3. Cancellations or no-shows that never recovered.

4. Enquiries that showed intent but never booked.

5. Useful appointment capacity sitting empty.

My instinct is to start where intent is already strongest and the evidence is easiest to verify.

But the answer changes by business.

A packed clinic with weak rebooking is different from a salon with repeated quiet Tuesday afternoons.

A practice with a huge enquiry volume is different from one losing regulars.

The useful part is not picking the same leak every time.

It is learning to identify which missed-revenue moment is actually worth solving first.

posts.title: The seven questions I would ask before building anything

copy.default:
Before I would build a Revenue Recovery system, I would want seven answers.

1. Where is the client dropping out?

2. What evidence says the gap is real?

3. How much intent already existed?

4. Is the timing still commercially relevant?

5. Can the right people be contacted appropriately?

6. What should happen when they respond or book?

7. Is the realistic opportunity worth fixing?

Only then does implementation become interesting.

Maybe the answer is email.

Maybe SMS.

Maybe a booking change.

Maybe a staff handoff.

Maybe no new system at all.

That is the logic behind the Revenue Recovery Check.

Diagnose the missed-revenue moment first.

Make the solution earn its place second.

posts.title: Why I do not want to sell automation first

copy.default:
I do not want to sell automation first.

Because once you start with the tool, every problem begins to look like something the tool should solve.

I would rather start with the missed-revenue moment.

What happened?

Why did it happen?

Is it recurring?

Is it commercially meaningful?

What would a good next state look like?

Only then ask whether automation helps.

Sometimes it will.

Sometimes a staff process is better.

Sometimes the booking journey needs changing.

Sometimes the opportunity is too small to justify building anything.

That makes the sales conversation less convenient.

It also makes the recommendation more credible.

If “do nothing” is allowed to win, the solution has to earn its place.

posts.title: The simplest definition of a Client Return System

copy.default:
The simplest definition I have found for a Client Return System is this:

Know who should come back.

Notice when the expected journey breaks.

Decide whether action is useful.

Make the next step easier.

Stop when the job is done.

Measure what happened.

That is it.

The technology underneath can become sophisticated.

CRM fields.

Segments.

Automations.

Waitlists.

Booking logic.

Attribution.

Dashboards.

But the operating idea should stay simple.

A valuable client relationship should not be allowed to quietly disappear just because nobody noticed the moment when the next step stopped happening.
